title: WorldFixture service manifest v1
description: One language-neutral service declaration. A valid manifest plus the contract tests is enough to add a service; no core registration is required. Revised after the first four services were described by it, which found three things the first draft could not say: that a service answers on several protocols and needs one readiness check per protocol; that the supervisor, not the image, allocates the ports and supplies the environment; and that an implementation can serve an upstream surface it does not own, which a resolver cannot see because a `provides` list only ever adds. Hence `readiness` also accepting a list, `ports` and `environment`, and `disclaims`. Every field added in that revision is optional, so a manifest written against the first draft still validates.

image.description: An immutable image reference. A lock never follows a mutable tag. Omitted when the service runs as a child process inside the one default image, where `command` is the whole answer.

container.description: How to run this service as a local container when its system packages are not installed in the checkout environment. `image` is the published, digest-pinned form; this is the buildable one, and the digest of what was actually built is recorded against the run rather than in the lock. A service can also declare `command`: checkout mode uses this container, while the all-in-one image uses the command and never starts Docker inside Docker.

build.description: A build context, relative to the service directory.

ports.description: Every port this service opens, named. `readiness[].port`, `ui.port` and `provides[].port` all reference a name from this list, so without it those fields point at nothing. The supervisor allocates a host port for each entry and writes the result into `env`; a service is not required to accept a bind address separately, and says so by omitting `bind_env`.

container_port.description: The default this image ships, used when the service runs unsupervised. A service whose ports are wholly supplied by the supervisor has none.

env.description: The environment variable the supervisor sets to open this port.

env_format.description: How the value is written. `port` is a bare number; `host_port` is `<bind>:<port>` in one variable, which is what a service with no separate bind_env expects.

container_loopback.description: Keep this private port on container loopback. Do not publish it; readiness runs inside the container.

published.description: Whether the target application reaches this port. A private back channel binds loopback and is never printed as a binding.

optional.description: True when the service starts without this port and giving it one enables the surface it serves. The composer works this way -- a vendor with no port is not started -- so a run pays for what it uses. False, the default, means the process will not start without it: SeaweedFS needs its master, volume and filer ports whether or not an application calls them.

environment.description: Values the supervisor owns and the service reads. Naming them here is what lets one supervisor start a service it has no built-in knowledge of, which is the whole claim of this contract.

from.description: `world.path` is the mounted artifact directory; `world.sha256` its content digest; `runtime.token` the private token the service uses to reach the runtime; `runtime.state` is the private per-instance state directory; `constant` takes `value`; `generated` takes a stable project-local value named by `key`.

readiness.description: Protocol-level readiness checks, not process liveness checks, and not a marker file written once at startup: a check must re-answer on every poll. A multi-protocol service declares one check per protocol that must be answering before the runtime calls it ready. The single-object form is the original draft and still validates.

provides.description: Exact named profiles. There is no global 'provider compatible' claim; each profile maps to contract tests.

port.description: Which of this service's ports serves the profile. Required in practice for any service with more than one port, or the resolver cannot turn a capability into a binding.

binds.description: The attributes an environment specification may bind to, as `<profile>/<name>`. Without these an environment's `bindings` block names an attribute nothing defines.

from.description: Port bindings are computed from the profile's port. `port.connection_url` also uses the declared scheme and local service credentials. `projection` reads `pointer` out of this service's projection, which is how a per-person credential is resolved without putting one in the manifest. `generated` takes a stable project-local value named by `key`. `projection.credential` reads a secret reference from the projection and resolves it from run credentials.

per_person.description: True when the attribute resolves differently for each world person, such as a Slack token.

requires.description: Capabilities this profile needs internally. The resolver selects them with the profile and gives the selected binding to this service through the named environment variable.

disclaims.description: Surfaces this implementation serves and does not support. A `provides` list is a declaration, and a resolver cannot see a route a service never mentions -- so a service that carries an upstream surface it does not own must say so here, and the resolver must either disable that port or refuse the pairing. Written because `@emulators/aws` serves a live, writable `/s3/` while SeaweedFS is the S3 owner.

projection.description: The one artifact projection this service loads before readiness. Use `projections` instead when a service reads more than one file, or reads part of a file another service owns.

projections.description: Every artifact file this service reads, and which part of each it owns. A file may appear in two services' manifests only when their subtrees are disjoint; the resolver checks that.

subtree.description: A JSON pointer to the part this service owns. Absent means the whole file.

verified.description: Whether this service checks the file's digest against the artifact manifest before using it.

lifecycle.description: What this service can actually do, over an interface something can call. A capability that exists in-process but is not exposed is not a lifecycle claim. A service that cannot export recoverable changes must say so; it cannot own rules that need guaranteed downstream delivery.

reset_mechanism.description: `restore` replays an exported snapshot and is exact whatever the seed clock did. `restart` re-runs the service and is exact only when it holds no wall-clock state. The release gate wants byte-equivalent starting projections, so the runtime has to know which it is getting.

clear_paths.description: Absolute, service-owned temporary paths the process runner clears before a restart reset. Container runs get a new writable layer instead.

snapshot_paths.description: State paths copied after accepted readiness and restored before restart. Runtime sockets and lock files must not be listed.

ui.description: An optional service UI on its own origin. It must not read another service's credentials.

kind.description: `protocol` asks whether the surface is answering now and must re-answer on every poll. `seed_gate` asks whether startup finished loading the world and may be a marker written once, which is all that a shell entry point can offer. A service with mutable seeded state usually needs both: s3's filer document proves every declared object was stored, and only a call to the S3 port proves the store still answers. Defaults to `protocol`.

expect.description: What a ready answer looks like: an HTTP status, or the prefix of a protocol greeting such as `220` for SMTP or `* OK` for IMAP. A non-status value is matched against the response body, which is what distinguishes the route the check intends from any other route that also returns 200.

method.description: The HTTP method, when the cheapest honest answer is not a GET. Slack's `auth.test` answers `not_authed` on POST and 404 on GET, so a GET check would have proven only that something was listening.
